note.question: How may incorporating pooling as a test strategy change which patients should be prioritized for a test?
note.overview: Motivated by the persistent lack of testing capacity in the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, we study the question “who should be tested?” when there are general costs and rewards, testing capacity is strictly limited, tests have errors, and patients differ in their prior probability of being infected. We specifically study how the answer to that question changes when pooled testing, a method of grouping samples to conserve tests, is an option. This setting reflects the situation decision makers faced at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020.

source.quote: Problem definition: Motivated by the persistent lack of testing capacity in the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, we study the question “who should be tested?” when there are general costs and rewards, testing capacity is strictly limited, tests have errors, and patients differ in their prior probability of being infected.
This setting reflects the situation decision makers faced at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020.

Managers and policymakers should understand how characteristics of the test and the setting impact whether it is optimal to test patients who are deemed likely to test positive or those who are likely to test negative.

In the COVID- 19 setting, these results are especially relevant because, although most tests appear to have good specificity, sensitivity varies widely between different types of tests and even between different brands or formula­ tions of the same type of test (Br¨ummer et al. 2021).

The prior probability of infec­ tion is the ex ante probability that the person is infected, given what is known about the person at the time the sample is collected, which is to say that it is a forecast.

Although worldwide testing capacity increased gradually over the course of the pan­ demic, demand also increased with the continued spread of the disease and relaxation of the social dis­ tancing measures imposed at the earlier stages of the pandemic.

conditions: Specifically, we propose the following decision rule that is supported by the analytical results of Section 3. • When RP < RN: Compose as many pools as possible given the number of available tests.
